name: Amycretin
evidenceNote: Randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1 and phase 2 trials in several hundred people show large weight loss and lower blood sugar. Phase 3 trials started in 2026 and have not reported, so long-term safety and effects on health outcomes are unknown.
summary: Amycretin (now zenagamtide) is Novo Nordisk's one-molecule GLP-1 and amylin agonist for obesity and diabetes. It is in phase 3 and not approved.
keyTakeaway: Amycretin, now called zenagamtide, is a single Novo Nordisk peptide that activates both GLP-1 and amylin receptors, two hormone systems that each reduce appetite. In an early randomized trial, people on the 20 mg weekly injection lost 22.0% of body weight at 36 weeks while the placebo group gained 1.9%. A daily tablet version lowered HbA1c by up to 1.4 points in type 2 diabetes. Stomach side effects were common. It is not FDA-approved: phase 3 trials, including one against semaglutide, began in 2026 and will run for years. Nothing sold online under this name is the trial drug.

blocks.text: Amycretin is an experimental peptide drug from Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes. It now carries the international nonproprietary name zenagamtide, and newer publications and trial listings use that name [1].

Its distinguishing feature is that one molecule acts on two hormone systems. Semaglutide, the drug in Wegovy, acts on the GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor alone [8]. Amycretin pairs GLP-1 activity with amylin activity in a single peptide, so both signals arrive from one injection or one tablet [2].

It is being studied in two forms: a once-weekly subcutaneous (under the skin) injection and a once-daily tablet. Both have reached phase 3, the final stage of testing before a company can apply for approval [4].

GLP-1 is a gut hormone that helps regulate appetite and calorie intake, and its receptor sits in several brain areas that control eating [8]. Amylin is a second hormone, released by the same pancreatic cells that make insulin, in step with insulin after a meal. It slows the rate at which food leaves the stomach, suppresses glucagon (a hormone that raises blood sugar), and reduces food intake through the brain [9].

Amycretin is a unimolecular agonist, meaning a single peptide that switches on GLP-1, amylin, and calcitonin receptors at once [1]. The aim is for the two appetite signals to add together. Whether that beats existing single-target drugs is the question a head-to-head phase 3 trial against semaglutide is designed to answer [5].
No. Amycretin is an investigational drug and is not approved anywhere. It is available only to people enrolled in Novo Nordisk's clinical trials.

The first phase 3 trial, AMAZE 1, began in February 2026. It plans to enroll about 1,150 adults with obesity, randomized to one of four weekly doses or placebo alongside diet and exercise, with weight change measured at 84 weeks. Its primary completion date is listed as June 2029 [4]. Other phase 3 trials registered in 2026 include a head-to-head comparison with semaglutide [5], a study of the tablet form [6], a heart outcomes trial in people with established cardiovascular disease [7], and a type 2 diabetes trial against insulin glargine [10].

blocks.text: The injectable form was tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1b/2a study at one research center in Texas. Participants with a BMI of 27 to 39.9 received rising weekly doses for up to 36 weeks. Weight loss grew with dose and treatment length [2].

Those numbers come from small groups, and many participants dropped out, often for reasons the investigators judged unrelated to side effects [2]. Results from early trials of this size may not hold up in larger, longer phase 3 programs, so the phase 3 readouts will matter more than these.

The tablet form was first tested in a first-in-human study with treatment lasting up to 12 weeks, whose main purpose was safety. Across 144 participants, 62% reported at least one side effect, all mild or moderate, and most were gastrointestinal [3]. A larger 36-week phase 2 trial then gave daily tablets of 6, 25, or 50 mg to 186 adults with type 2 diabetes already taking metformin. HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over about three months) fell by 0.9, 1.3, and 1.4 percentage points from baseline, which was 0.5, 0.99, and 1.09 points more than placebo [1].

Side effects match those of other GLP-1 and amylin drugs. In the diabetes trial, gastrointestinal effects occurred in 26% to 47% of people taking amycretin depending on dose, against 23% on placebo [1]. Approved GLP-1 drugs carry label warnings for pancreatitis and gallbladder disease [8], and trials of amycretin so far are too small to show whether it shares those risks.

Some research chemical websites list powders labeled amycretin. The investigational drug is supplied only through registered studies such as AMAZE 1 [4], so anything bought online is a different, unregulated product of unknown identity and purity. Doses used in the trials cannot be assumed to apply to it.
